title: Act Boldly in an Uncertain World
overview: Because no one can know the future, the chapter urges people to act, give, work and enjoy life now, while remembering that life is brief and accountable to God.

parts.label: Sending out what you have (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Sending food across the water and splitting it among seven or eight shares may describe bold trade or generous giving, and interpreters have long read it both ways. Either way, since disaster may come, the advice is not to hoard or stake everything on one thing.

parts.label: Stop waiting for perfect weather (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: Full clouds rain and a fallen tree stays where it lands; some things just happen, beyond our control. A farmer who keeps watching the wind and clouds for the ideal moment never plants or harvests.

parts.label: What we cannot know (v. 5)
parts.note: The Hebrew word here can mean wind or spirit, and it stands beside the mystery of a baby forming in the womb. Just as these are hidden from us, so is the full picture of what God is doing.

parts.label: Keep working anyway (v. 6)
parts.note: Sow early and late, because you can't tell which effort will succeed, or whether both will. Not knowing is treated as a reason to stay busy, not to freeze.

parts.label: Enjoy the light (vv. 7-8)
parts.note: Light and life are good, so enjoy every year, but remember that many dark days will also come. The text leaves open whether these are hard times in life or old age and death, and it calls what lies ahead fleeting, using the book's key word for breath or vapor.

parts.label: Joy in youth, with accountability (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: Young people are told to enjoy their years and do what their hearts desire, but to know that God will hold them to account for how they live. Because youth passes like a breath, they should let go of worry and needless pain while it lasts.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether verse 9 is a sincere invitation to enjoy life within God's limits, as most modern scholars read it, or mainly an ironic warning against indulgence, as many older interpreters held.
think: When the future feels uncertain, does it make you more cautious or more willing to take chances, and what has shaped that in you?
